question.prompt: An equilateral triangle is drawn with a side of length \(a.\) A new equilateral triangle is formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of the first one. Then a third equilateral triangle is formed by joining the midpoints of the sides of the second; and so on forever. The limit of the sum of the perimeters of all the triangles thus drawn is:

solutions.explanation:
Let \(a>0\) be the original side length. A segment joining two side midpoints is half the length of the third side. Thus each new triangle has half the side length, and hence half the perimeter, of the preceding triangle. Including the original triangle, the perimeters are
\[
3a,\quad \frac{3a}{2},\quad \frac{3a}{4},\quad\ldots.
\]
Let \(S_n\) be the sum of the first \(n\) perimeters, where \(n\ge1\). Multiplying this sum by \(\frac12\) shifts the terms one place. Subtracting cancels all the intermediate terms:
\[
S_n-\frac12S_n=3a-\frac{3a}{2^n}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
S_n=6a\left(1-\frac1{2^n}\right).
\]
As \(n\) increases, \(2^{-n}\) tends to zero, so the limiting sum is \(6a\), choice D.
solutions.title: Sum the successively halved perimeters
